World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Farrer contest could remake the conservative side of politics
World.content:
It has been a long time since a by-election has garnered this much attention in the corridors of power.

Often, by-elections are seen as a chance for voters to whack the government in charge. More often than not, oppositions can whip up some anger and secure a swing towards them.

But instead, with the government not even fielding a candidate, this weekend's Farrer by-election has become a contest that could remake the conservative side of Australian politics.

The first electoral test for both new Coalition party leaders, Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan, sees the opposition at serious risk of losing Farrer for the first time since the seat was created in 1949.

A safe seat for decades

Although it has been passed back and forth between the Liberal and National parties, Farrer has been a safe Coalition seat for decades.

With Labor as the Coalition's primary opponent, it has held the seat on a margin of more than 10 per cent since 1984.

In the world of two-party politics, the opposition has been able to take Farrer as a given. But now, voters have other serious options.

This by-election is a single-seat diorama of the squeeze that the Coalition currently finds itself in nationally.

On one side, One Nation is trying to prove it can break through and win its first-ever federal lower house seat at an election, and this by-election represents a very good opportunity to do so, at a very good time.

Nationally, the party has been consistently polling ahead of the Coalition for months.

The other side of the squeeze comes from independent Michelle Milthorpe, who is making a second tilt at the seat.

In last year's federal election, she came closer to victory than Labor has managed in more than 50 years.

Milthorpe was quick out the blocks when Sussan Ley announced she would leave parliament, declaring her candidacy within hours.

The Nationals are also contesting, making this a complex race.

Farrer is big. Real big

Covering more than 126,000 square kilometres, Farrer is larger than Iceland and South Korea, and nearly as big as Greece.

About a third of the seat's population lives in Albury along the border, but Farrer also takes in historic towns in the Riverina like Griffith and Leeton, a chain of border towns along the Murray, and remote areas along the western edge of the state.

A trained pilot, Ley got around the electorate by air.

The demographic diversity means we'll likely see different candidates performing well in different parts of Farrer: Milthorpe may poll strongly in Albury but less well outside the city.

In fact, if Farrer only contained Albury, Milthorpe would've won last year.

On the other hand, One Nation is likely to perform better in the smaller towns and remote parts of the seat, where you would otherwise think the Nationals would be strongest.

The stakes are high on all sides: One Nation is desperate to prove itself at the federal level, after more than one in five South Australians gave the party their first preference in the state's election in March.

The party also won nearly a quarter of the primary vote in the state seat of Nepean last weekend, on Victoria's Mornington Peninsula.

One Nation needs a good result here to show that their national polling can actually win them seats in parliament.

If Pauline Hanson's party fails to win Farrer, where else could it win seats?

And if it succeeds, then it has most likely done so on a night where both coalition partners have been separately clobbered by different opponents, pushing them into third and fourth place on the primary vote.

It would show a struggling Coalition failing to keep its broad church together while preachers outside, unconstrained by the need for compromise, pick off the once faithful.

In the end, how many people will be left sitting on the Coalition's pews?

What's at stake for the Nationals?

Much of the focus of this by-election has been the fate of the Liberal Party, with comparatively less time spent discussing the National Party's prospects.

From the very beginning, the Nationals were downbeat on their chances in this seat, and polling during the campaign suggests the party is struggling to get out of the single digits.

That would be an extraordinary result given the history of the seat.

In 2001, when Ley was first elected to parliament, she won in a very tight contest against the National Party. Up to that point Farrer had been held by party giant Tim Fischer for just under 17 years.

Since then, the Nationals haven't contested the seat, as required by the Coalition agreement with the Liberals. But Farrer has retained its regional character and new Nationals leader Matt Canavan has spent a lot of time in the seat throughout the campaign.

One Nation winning Farrer would arguably raise larger questions for the Nationals than the Liberals, because this seat lies smack bang in the middle of Nationals heartland.

The party holds four of the five neighbouring seats in New South Wales and Victoria.

The fifth seat is Indi, which is now held by independent Helen Haines.

The inland New South Wales seats of Calare and New England also have a long history with the National Party.

With the exception of Calare, which former National Andrew Gee retained in last year's election after his move to the crossbench, these are seats that the Nationals easily held last year.

The most marginal Nationals-held seat in New South Wales is on a margin of 12.6 per cent.

But if the combined Coalition vote in Farrer has, as the limited polling suggests, fallen below 30 per cent, all of those MPs could have a fight on their hands.

Do Nationals MPs like Michael McCormack, Sam Birrell and Anne Webster have cause for concern in the lead-up to the next general election? We'll get some clues on Saturday.

This Saturday Angus Taylor's party may lose a seat.

Matt Canavan's party may lose its heartland.

World.title: 'We still have no idea': RBA warns of harsh Iran war reality
World.content:
Australia had an inflation problem before the Iran war, but it's turned sinister.

Prior to the war, core inflation — which the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) focuses on in its interest rate decisions — was well above 3 per cent.

But the RBA wants inflation to be at or around 2.5 per cent.

Enter the Iran war, an effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a major oil price spike, and headline monthly inflation has surged to 4.6 per cent.

"Higher fuel prices are adding to inflation, and there are indications that this is likely to have second-round effects on prices for goods and services more broadly," the RBA's Monetary Policy Board said in its post-decision statement yesterday.

"It is tough, and we're staring down the barrel. It is a tough time," RBA governor Michele Bullock acknowledged later at a press conference.

Michele Bullock has been steadfast in her warnings about the need to control inflation. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

Australia has become hostage to the oil price spike and, as Bullock puts it, it means "we are all feeling poorer".

The problem facing the nation is that there is no clear solution or end in sight to Australia's worsening inflation problem.

The Middle East conflict, Ms Bullock said, had "complicated things immensely".

But it's more than that.

The war, with its daily twists and turns, means the RBA will be largely flying blind on monetary policy until the Strait of Hormuz is opened for the safe passage of ships.

"Certainly, when I stood here in March, I think the war was maybe a week or two old, and everyone was thinking it'll be over in a couple of weeks," Bullock said.

"It isn't. We're still here, we still have no idea."

RBA commentary shifts

There has been a material shift in the commentary around the March interest rates decision.

Earlier this year, the RBA was concerned that demand in the economy was greater than supply.

The backdrop to this was weak productivity, such that the economy's speed limit had lowered.

In this environment, it's practically impossible to achieve higher levels of economic growth without speeding and pushing inflation higher.

"Information since the February meeting suggests that some of the increase in inflation reflects greater capacity pressures," the March Monetary Policy Board statement read.

Excess demand in the economy has led to an inflation problem.

Now, the oil shock has exacerbated the inflation problem and, as a result, "we are all feeling poorer, that's what this war has done to us", Bullock said.

Today's rates rise will result in another impost on household budgets. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

It's almost insulting

Supply constraints, or the economy's ability to produce stuff, have led to higher inflation and tighter monetary policy — not indulgent mortgage borrowers spending big.

Now, a war halfway across the world is adding to those cost pressures in the economy.

Donald Trump's actions in the Middle East are impacting economies around the world. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Supply constraints remain, and we now have bog-standard, cost-push inflation.

Again, it has nothing to do with excess spending by households with mortgages.

But, as we had heard ad nauseam, the RBA is trying to slow the economy to ease the part of the inflation problem it can control, and monetary policy is the only tool it has.

"Inflation hurts all Australians," Bullock said.

But there are degrees of pain.

And it's plain to all that mortgage borrowers are shouldering the burden to tame inflation.

Inflation expectations

The bad news is the worst may be yet to come.

"The board assessed that inflation is likely to remain above target for some time and that the risks remain tilted to the upside, including to inflation expectations," the Monetary Policy Board said in its recent statement.

This is what the pundits call a "hawkish hold".

It means the latest interest rate hike could easily be followed by one or two more increases.

Although not necessarily next month, judging by this comment from the governor in her press conference: "One reason for deciding to increase interest rates, to give ourselves space now to sit and see what happens, whether the baseline turns out or it's an adverse scenario, that was part of the thinking."

Mortgage repayments calculator Our mortgage repayment calculator will show you how much your loan repayments may change.

The reason more rate rises remain on the agenda is that the RBA is not just worried about the possible ongoing effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

It's worried that, right now, shoppers are making the logical leap in their minds that prices are going to increase at a faster pace over the weeks and months ahead.

In response, they are going to increase their spending now to avoid those higher prices.

This brings demand forward and adds to inflationary pressures in the economy.

It can easily feed on itself, too.

The Monetary Policy Board noted this week that "short-term measures of inflation expectations" had already risen.

It also said that a "longer or more severe conflict could put further upward pressure on global energy prices".

Cargo ships near the Strait of Hormuz, as viewed from a rocky shoreline in the United Arab Emirates last week. (AP: Fatima Shbair)

"This will push up near-term inflation and could also increase inflation further out if it impairs supply capacity or price rises get built into longer-term inflation expectations," the statement read.

It's an economically ugly place to be in.

Loading

Recession risks loom

An inflation problem is unfortunate. A fast-paced inflation problem is an extreme challenge.

That's because it will likely be practically impossible for the RBA to bring inflation to heel under an inflation breakout scenario without pushing the country into recession.

"My view is that if the RBA did deliver two further rate hikes this year, we're likely facing a recession," Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said.

"Will that be needed? We can only hope not."

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver has similar concerns.

"The longer the strait remains closed, the greater the odds of a severe bout of stagflation, with inflation well above 5 per cent and recession," Dr Oliver said.

"The full implications of the implied 10–15 per cent hit to global oil and gas supply will become apparent as oil reserves run down."

RBA risks recession Monetary policy trade-offs are getting worse — the Reserve Bank of Australia is confronting rising inflation and downgraded growth forecasts. And there's nothing much it can do.

A recession is widely regarded as two consecutive quarters of negative growth in gross domestic product (GDP), or put another way, six months of economic contraction.

But it's typically accompanied by surging unemployment.

In Australia, that would likely mean an unemployment rate above 5 per cent.

So it was ominous when Bullock said: "I hope we can keep unemployment in the fours."

"So far the RBA seems to be far more optimistic on the jobs market and has only raised its forecasts slightly for the unemployment rate — with it now rising to 4.7 per cent by the end of the forecast horizon, from 4.6 per cent previously," HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham noted.

The RBA's catch 22 is clear.

At the heart of the economic dilemma is businesses' ability to pass on higher costs over the coming weeks and months.

As Bullock put it: "You'd be wrong to expect that businesses would not look to pass on some of the costs of doing business."

"Otherwise, if they can't, then what's going to happen to the businesses?" she said.

"Then you will end up in a recession."

Or as CreditorWatch chief economist Ivan Colhoun said: "Either way, the combination of higher interest rates and higher energy prices will add to pressures not only on household budgets, but also on the costs of doing business."

"This is likely to result in some increase in insolvencies in the months ahead unless a peace agreement can be reached relatively soon," he said.

For both businesses and households under pressure, the clock is ticking.

World.title: 'Straw that broke the camel's back': Financial distress grows as rates rise
World.content:
More than 65,000 Australians have contacted the National Debt Helpline in financial distress since the start of the year, with most callers saying they are struggling to pay their home loans.

Yesterday, the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates for a third time this year by 0.25 percentage points, taking the official cash rate from 4.10 per cent to 4.35 per cent, leaving many borrowers increasingly worried about how they will come up with the extra cash when budgets are already so tight.

Bianca Gambrill's mortgage repayments have increased by more than $600 a fortnight since she bought her home during the COVID pandemic.

The teacher from Newcastle in NSW said making the repayments had become increasingly challenging.

"We make the minimum repayments … which means, because we didn't buy until our 40s … if we keep at this rate, we're paying off our home loan into our 70s," she told the ABC.

Recently, Ms Gambrill had to take out a credit card to cover her dog's vet bills and still has not paid it off.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this story please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com

"We went into quite significant credit card debt to do it, so I've got a $10,000 credit card debt there in order to meet those medical bills," she said.

"It's very stressful, there are a lot of really hard discussions about it because all of our money is going on the mortgage."

Ms Gambrill was diagnosed with ADHD as an adult and said interest rate hikes were also impacting when she could buy her medication.

"This year I've had to go off meds during school holidays so I can stretch them out as they are too expensive," she said.

Tens of thousands of people in 'distress' before latest rate hike

Financial counsellors say that as interest rates rise, it is not just vulnerable people but many employed people and young families who are feeling the impacts.

The data shows in April 2026, there were 13,933 calls to the National Debt Helpline. That compares to 11,554 callers in April 2025.

RBA risks recession Monetary policy trade-offs are getting worse — the Reserve Bank of Australia is confronting rising inflation and downgraded growth forecasts. And there's nothing much it can do.

The latest interest rate hike yesterday is set to tip more Australians into housing stress, financial counsellors warn.

The majority of those contacting the helpline over the past few months are people facing mortgage stress — typically where more than 30 per cent of their income is being spent on paying their home loan.

While mortgage stress is the main reason, other reasons people contact the helpline include credit card debt, electricity bills, debts owed to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), and personal loans.

Financial counsellors said the rising cost of fuel was also becoming a major issue, especially for people in rural and remote areas.

Financial Counselling Australia CEO Domenique Meyrick said it had been the busiest start to the year.

"If we compare it to last April, we've had a 21 per cent increase in calls and a 45 per cent increase in people using the chat function — that's a significant increase," she said.

Domenique Meyrick says the latest rate hike will "sting" for those already doing it tough. (ABC News: Simon Winter )

Ms Meyrick said recent data showed 41 per cent of people contacting National Debt Helpline were in some type of employment — 28 per cent in full-time and 14 per cent in part-time.

She said 34 per cent had dependents and 27 per cent were in the 35-44 age bracket.

"People in full-time employment, people in part-time employment, people with children, people from all the parts of our community are really doing it tough at the moment," she said.

"For that group of people who are already in financial difficulty and have a mortgage, an interest rate hike always stings.

" For some people, it [the latest rate hike] will be the straw that broke the camel's back. "

Loading...

Other bills go unpaid

As recession fears grow, Ms Meyrick said people were avoiding defaulting on their mortgages by cutting back on other essentials.

"A lot of people will prioritise their housing over everything else, so they will not pay their telephone bills or their energy bills, they'll go without meals, they will skip medical appointments," Ms Meyrick said.

"They do pretty much whatever they can to make sure they meet those housing costs and so by the time people have come to seek the support of a financial counsellor often … they've got no discretionary spending at all."

People facing difficulty making mortgage repayments should reach out to their lenders for help, counsellors advise, as do the banks themselves.

"Pick up the phone and call your bank early and say, 'Hey, I'm on the edge of financial difficulty, I need some support here', ask for hardship [relief]," she said.

More than 1.6 million Australians 'at risk' of mortgage stress

Separate data released in late April from Roy Morgan showed that with the RBA raising the cash rate to 4.35 per cent, the share of borrowers "at risk" of mortgage stress is forecast to rise to 30.4 per cent, equivalent to 1.64 million people.

If the RBA raises rates again in June by 0.25 percentage points to 4.6 per cent, the share of borrowers at risk would increase to 30.9 per cent, equivalent to 1.67 million people, up 219,000 from before the May and June rate hikes.

The RBA has lifted interest rates for a third time this year. (Reuters: Jason Reed)

Roy Morgan's data considers borrowers at risk if they paying more than a certain proportion of their after-tax household income (25 per cent to 45 per cent depending on income and spending) into their home loan.

Roy Morgan chief executive Michele Levine said it was not interest rates but unemployment that had the biggest impact on income and mortgage stress.

"It's if they lose their job or main source of income," she said, adding that an ongoing war in the Middle East would increase inflation.

Roy Morgan data shows more Australians are at risk of mortgage stress as interest rates rise. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Banks call on people in distress to get in touch early

The major banks say while stressed lending and housing delinquency rates are still relatively low, more Australians are building buffers or getting in contact about repayment options before they default on their mortgages.

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullocks speaks following the RBA rates rise to 4.35% on 5 May 2026. (ABC News)

ANZ chief financial officer Farhan Faruqi told a recent investor briefing that mortgage customers' delinquencies decreased three basis points in the half to 83 basis points.

"Our mortgage customers continue to show resilience with 88 per cent of accounts ahead on repayments, and approximately 70 per cent of customers holding savings buffers of three months or more," he said.

He said the bank had not seen a material increase in customer requests for hardship relief but was "very conscious of the stress from higher interest rates and cost-of-living pressures" and was closely monitoring it.

A Westpac spokeswoman said 85 per cent of customers were ahead on their mortgage repayments.

Recession or inflation? If there's any certainty about the RBA's interest rate verdict, it's that it will be a split decision.

Only 0.53 per cent of Westpac's total mortgage portfolio of $518 billion (excluding its RAMS business) was experiencing financial hardship and the bank was offering options for them, including deferred or reduced repayments.

Of those who are in a hardship arrangement, the most common support provided was a temporary pause on repayments (66 per cent) or temporary reduced repayments (16 per cent).

Property research group Cotality could not provide data on distressed home sales but said there had been a more obvious trend towards auctions being withdrawn from the market prior to going ahead.

This week, the preliminary numbers showed 18.3 per cent of auctions were withdrawn without a rescheduled date.

Cotality said the increase in withdrawn auctions likely represented less confidence from sellers to test the market under auction conditions, probably due to low numbers of registered bidders leading up to the auction event, or feedback from the market that vendor price expectations would not be achieved.

World.title: More than eight million Australians now receive income support
World.content:
More than eight million Australians now rely on some form of income support, putting pressure on a safety net that was never designed to take on so many, but insurers say earlier intervention and unified assessment processes would improve the system.

With around two million more people now accessing payments than a decade ago, the surge is being driven by Australians whose physical and mental health has deteriorated to the point they can no longer work.

Mental ill health now accounts for about one-third of claims across Australia's major income support schemes, according to data compiled by researchers at Monash University and SuperFriend for the Council of Australian Life Insurers (CALI).

"We are now faced with a major national productivity challenge," said Christine Cupitt, chief executive of CALI.

" It's not just one part of the system under pressure — the entire safety net is under strain. "

CEO of CALI, Christine Cupitt, says the entire system is under pressure. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

The report found demand had increased across all 11 of Australia's income support systems, spanning employer-provided sick leave and workers' compensation to social security payments, superannuation and life insurance claims.

Employers remain the biggest contributor, with paid sick leave supporting around 7.5 million Australians, typically for short periods of about three weeks.

However, more people are exhausting sick leave and moving into longer term support, where the chances of returning to work diminish.

"Mental health has really changed the profile of these claims," Ms Cupitt said.

"It's now one of the leading drivers of people needing income support, and these claims tend to be more complex and longer in duration."

'It took me completely by surprise'

For 30‑year-old Lauren Frahamer, the statistics are reflected in her daily life, after long COVID meant she could no longer work.

Before she fell ill, Ms Frahamer was a stage manager on major musical theatre productions, working around 50 hours a week, often nights and weekends, while maintaining an intense fitness routine of gym sessions, swimming, running and yoga.

"I was very active," she said. "Work was a big part of my life."

She contracted COVID in December 2021, during an outbreak that spread through her workplace.

Ms Frahamer says fear and confusion set in as symptoms dragged on. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

The acute illness was brutal but unremarkable — weeks of fever, pain and exhaustion — but recovery never came.

"I tried to go back to work for about a month and just couldn't do it," she said.

"I had extreme fatigue. I had brain fog. I couldn't remember a sentence well enough to pass a message on. My job depends on focus for hours at a time, and I just didn't have it."

As the symptoms dragged on, Ms Frahamer said confusion and fear set in.

"I was mentally unwell through that whole process," she said.

"At first, I was almost numb. Then as my brain started coming back online, I realised something was seriously wrong.

"I hadn't had a major health event before — it took me completely by surprise."

What is income protection insurance? People often — wrongly — believe income protection insurance would be paid out if the person was unable to work due to losing their job for any reason.

Eventually, she resigned, moved back to Melbourne to be closer to family, and began treatment through an allied health clinic specialising in complex, long-term conditions.

The turning point came when her partner at the time was made redundant.

"That's when I really had to look at what support existed," she said.

"I didn't even know if long COVID would be recognised. I had no idea if it was claimable."

Ms Frahamer now works nine hours a week from home in client support. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

In mid-2022, Ms Frahamer was granted partial income protection — support she said kept her from losing independence altogether.

"It didn't take long to burn through my savings," she said.

"Rent, life costs, appointments, medications — it adds up fast. Without income protection, I would've had to move back in with my parents and be completely dependent again."

Ms Frahamer now works nine hours a week in client support at the same allied health clinic that once treated her — about 40 per cent of her former capacity.

"It's been about a year at this level," she said.

But she's determined to take steps to work full-time again.

"Work gives you purpose," she said.

"When it's taken away through no fault of your own … it's hard."

Earlier intervention needed

Associate Professor Ross Iles, a Monash University researcher and chief research adviser at SuperFriend, said the number of working-age Australians needing income support had risen steadily.

"Mental health seems to be having a bigger toll on people's ability to work," he said.

One of the biggest problems with the way income support is set up is fragmentation, according to Mr Iles.

Close to $80 billion a year is being spent on income support. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Each scheme has different eligibility rules, medical evidence requirements and application processes.

"If someone's workers' compensation claim is rejected and they need to turn to insurance or social security, that's a whole new application," he said.

"New forms, new medical assessments, new processes. When you're unwell, that burden is enormous."

Mental health issues amongst workers sees huge spike in insurance claims Over a 10-year period, mental health claims by Australian workers aged between 30 and 40 have increased by more than 730 per cent, new data has revealed.

He said the longer a person was out of work, the less likely they were to return. Delays in treatment, claim processing and coordinated support reduced recovery prospects and increased long-term costs.

"We're spending close to $80 billion a year on income support," Mr Iles said.

" And that figure doesn't even count lost productivity. The best outcome is helping people stay connected to work or return when they can. "

Life insurers say the current system intervenes too late.

They're calling for earlier, better-coordinated support while people are still working as well as a government-led overhaul that links Australia's 11 income support systems to employers, insurers and public agencies.

It would mean nationally consistent mental ‑health definitions, shared data, better identification of people at risk of long-term work loss, and smoother transitions between supports.

"There's a burning platform here," Ms Cuppitt said.

"We can't afford systems operating in silos while more Australians get sick and leave the workforce."

World.title: How a flamboyant thief quietly pulled off an extraordinary coin heist
World.content:
Coins, for most people — or at least those old enough to recognise actual physical currency without the assistance of a parent — are a deeply mundane affair.

They're a signifier of value, nothing more. You swap them for stuff you want: a cup of coffee, a chocolate bar, a phone call. Occasionally a coin might also help you unlock a jammed dunny door, or open a beer, or quantify your luck on the scratchies.

For a small but extremely focused slice of the human population, though, coins — rare ones, ancient ones — sing with a siren song inaudible to the rest of us. The itch to acquire such coins, to hoard them, to possess them at all costs, can in rare cases become so unscratchable that even the criminal codes offer scant deterrence.

Such is the case of David Gee, who in the late 1960s and early 1970s pulled off one of the most baroque and ambitious coin heists in Australian history, in which he nicked incredibly precious coins from the special collections of Australia's oldest library without anybody noticing.

The tale is featured in a new episode of ABC Listen's podcast, History Or Hoarding?.

Annabel Crabb explores the collections of the State Library of NSW in the new podcast, History or Hoarding? (ABC: Julia O'Shea)

What makes this story of subterfuge so extraordinary is that, in the Sydney of the late 1960s, which is where this tale is largely set, Gee himself was a highly noticeable person.

Flamboyant, sociable and generous, Gee ran a Kings Cross restaurant, enjoyed ballroom dancing, had a difficult-to-pin-down interest in the adult entertainment sector, and was utterly obsessed with coins. He'd developed the coin itch very young; having emigrated from China in 1939 with his parents at the age of 10, he was by his teenage years managing the books for the family's fruit and vegetable grocery business and diverting money wherever he could toward the acquisition of rare and collectable currency.

"Whenever he did things or talked to you, it was almost, ah, mesmerising," says Jim Noble, a celebrated Sydney numismatist and dealer who knew Gee.

"You couldn't get a word in. He was that excited about his coins, and he had a lot of good coins."

The pseudonyms

Noble himself became a coin freak as a boy. He still recalls at age 13 going to the cinema with his mother, still high on the excitement of buying his first rare coin — a "Gun Money" shilling minted by James II during the Williamite War in Ireland.

"I remember I sat on the end of the row seat where there was a little light and I kept getting my coin out and looking at it," he says.

Gee was every bit as passionate as Noble, but much more ethically ambiguous. And his urge to acquire rare coins took him, in the late 1960s, to the State Library of NSW — more particularly, the library's Dixson Collection. Named for benefactor William Dixson, a fervent collector and heir to a tobacco empire, the collection contains around 8,000 coins, notes and medals and a vast trove of Australiana.

Inside the State Library of NSW. (ABC: Sophie Kesteven)

Gee used the pseudonym "Robert Lowe" to register with the library's Special Collections division. It was one of more than 70 names he would adopt over the course of his life, the most swashbuckling of which was "Goldfinger". (In the online numismatic chat rooms where Gee is legendary, one participant recalls meeting him at a coin auction and asking him to autograph a copy of the 1986 hardcover, Heads I Win: The True Story of David Gee, Australia's Most Audacious Coin Forger. “Which name do you want me to sign?” the ever-suave Gee is reported to have asked.)

In an oral history recorded by the State Library of NSW in 2005, and which has since slumbered in the library's vast collection, librarian Joy Storie described "Mr Lowe" as an unforgettable and "very cheery" visitor who'd appear each morning.

"A loud booming voice would stride in … he would slap people on the back, whether that's staff or readers. And most of us responded with a big smile back, but [Dixson librarian] Bess Cook used to cringe, because she liked absolute quiet in the library."

"Mr Lowe" was always squeaky clean, Storie said. "He smelled a bit like Lifebuoy soap. And he always looked as if he'd just finished pressing his shirt. Always a blue shirt. Tucked in."

The cover story

The cover story proffered by "Mr Lowe" was that he was writing a book about Australian coins. In any other institution, such a pretext might have raised eyebrows. But in the library, where oddballs pursuing niche research topics are common, it was drab plumage indeed.

His presence was irritating to the librarians, though.

Like any taxpayer, "Mr Lowe" was entitled to request assistance to view anything in the library's collection. He wanted to see the coins. And because of their value, library rules dictated that he never be left alone with them.

It fell to Storie to spend what seemed like endless days monitoring "Mr Lowe" in a small room as he photographed and examined tray after tray of precious colonial-era Australian coins.

At Christmas, he windmilled in with bottles of French champagne for the staff. Dixson librarian Bess Cook was scandalised, insisting that they could not accept gifts or blandishments. A librarian was sent to pursue "Mr Lowe" and return the fizz. But he escaped.

The Dixson Collection contains around 8,000 coins, notes and medals and a vast trove of Australiana. (ABC: Sophie Kesteven)

What we now know is that David Gee — having studied and photographed the coins in the Dixson collection that he most deeply craved — then embarked on the next phase of his scheme.

Working under another assumed name with craftspeople across the engraving sector, he designed and commissioned replicas of the coins.

And when he next returned to the library, according to Joy Storie's account, it was with a genuinely preposterous new gambit.

"Well, time passed and I don't know what month it was… but it was after November anyway, because he came in and said that on Guy Fawkes' Night, his son — one of his sons — had inadvertently set fire [to] the study with a firecracker, and his photographic collection had gone up in flames and he would now have to rephotograph all the coins."

The switcheroo

After some debate and consternation, it was decided that this irritating numismatist could not be denied.

But this time, he brought different equipment: an improved camera set-up, which he said lit the coins better as he photographed them. The camera now had a plywood box cover, and he needed to place the coins inside the box to photograph them, obscuring the items briefly from the direct view of the supervising librarian.

With hindsight, of course, it is readily apparent that "Mr Lowe" was pulling a switcheroo worthy of only the lowest-grade trainee magician.

A deeply suspicious Joy Storie flagged the development with superiors at the time, but he was approved to continue.

And it wasn't until several years later — on March 16, 1973, when the library brought out a tempting selection of numismatic treats for a one-day-only exhibition for a fleet of coin experts visiting Sydney — that the first unmistakable whiff of disaster was detected.

David Gee was obsessed with Australian gold coins, such as this 1853 Port Phillip Kangaroo Office piece. The State Library of NSW still holds Gee forgeries, and it takes a numismatist to spot the difference. (ABC: Sophie Kesteven)

Melbourne numismatist Ray Jewell (yes, nominative determinism seems to play as rich a role among collectors of rarities as it does among librarians, see among others: Joy Storie) in what is now a famous moment, leaned in for a second look at a tray of early colonial gold coins and, according to Jim Noble, wondered aloud: "Oh, that's very nice. But, um, when are we gonna see the real ones?"

A good forger — and by this stage of his career David Gee was very good — can craft a replica that is undetectable to all but the most practised eyes.

The library brought in experts to check through the Dixson collection. This process was inexact because the collection, being so vast, had not been catalogued fully. It took years to establish how many Gee fakes it contained. Certainly more than 30. Probably more.

And Gee's exploits were not limited to the library; his deep contacts in the coin community and even at the Mint meant that by the 1970s, Gee fakes were sloshing about everywhere.

A bullshit artist and an artist-artist

After a mesmerising criminal trial, Gee was jailed in 1979, and the collecting institutions across Australia felt a shiver of apprehension.

The library's catalogue is now unimpeachably thorough, and the coins live in the Strong Room, a secure fortress deep underground at the Macquarie Street site (some of the coins were used in evidence at Gee's trial). You can view a small collection of Gee forgeries at the National Mint.

Half a century after the theft, the story of Gee and his trickery is still a nightmare-inducing story everybody at the library knows. They're only just ready to joke about it.

"We have a new access rule. No one who looks at the coins is allowed to have any clothing on," deadpans Maggie Patten, a veteran librarian, as she handles sheet after sheet of Dixson coins in the Strong Room.

And here's the thing: Gee forgeries are much prized in the coin collecting world. Not because they're the real thing, but because they carry such a comet-trail of story behind them. David Gee was certainly a bullshit artist, but he was also an artist artist.

Two Holey Dollars and one Dump. These coins were made by punching the middle out of a Spanish colonial silver dollar and the new details were stamped in. (ABC: Sophie Kesteven)

And Australian currency itself is in no position to disparage Gee. Its own story was born of criminality.

In the early days of the NSW colony, there was no local currency. Settlers got by with any British, Portuguese or Spanish currency they could scrounge, plus rum and promissory notes. It was an extremely ramshackle system.

Governor Macquarie resolved to strike a currency for the colony; he imported 40,000 silver Spanish dollars and puzzled over how to make them unique to NSW.

Fortunately for Macquarie, there was an expert already resident in Sydney, William Henshall, who oversaw the process of punching doughnut holes out of each coin, thus doubling the number that could go into circulation, and stamping them clearly with their new values: Five shillings for the doughnuts, 15 pence for the "dump", the smaller coin.

And how is it that William Henshall, an imaginative and deft designer and maker of coins, just happened to be in Sydney at the exact moment that Governor Macquarie found himself in need of this skill set?

Mr Henshall was in Sydney because he'd been deported from England in 1806, having been convicted of… forgery.

Listen to History Or Hoarding? at ABC Listen or wherever you find your podcasts.

World.title: This comic wowed Edinburgh Fringe. Now she's getting a handle on love
World.content:
Elouise Eftos has never been in love.

"I don't know if it's real," the award-winning Greek Australian comedian says. "There's a part of me that wants to believe it's real, but I don't know if it's possible for me."

That's the starting point for Aphrodite, the latest show from 32-year-old Eftos, whose 2024 debut hour was called Australia's First Attractive Comedian.

It's an assertion that earned Eftos both fans and naysayers, including My Big Fat Greek Wedding writer and star Nia Vardalos, who said the comedian was "taking us back to the dark ages", or fellow comics who thought the name implied they were ugly.

"I'm not making fun of women," Eftos says. "I'm making fun of how you see women." (Supplied: Century)

"You guys can go on stage and say you're hot," Eftos says. "I never said 'female' [comedian].

"It's a marketing thing. It's funny and it grabs people's attention."

Rather than putting other comics down, Eftos was trying to make her comedy persona "high status", rather than self-deprecating, perhaps the dominant style of comedy in Australia.

"I don't watch women that self-deprecate on stage and feel empowered," she says.

"I watched so many women talk down about themselves and I saw men go on stage and talk shit about women. So, everybody talks shit about women."

Instead, Eftos, who grew up in Perth and felt she didn't fit into conventional beauty ideals, wanted to send up antiquated ideas about who gets to be funny and confident on stage.

Quickly, her "silly joke" became a kind of affirmation.

"I grew up as a wog in the 90s," she says. "I wasn't blonde. I never thought I was beautiful. I never thought that guys liked me.

" It's a silly joke, but it's almost me being like: If I tell myself I'm hot and I'm smart and I'm funny, I'll believe it. "

Last year, Australia's First Attractive Comedian made Eftos the first Australian woman to land a best newcomer nomination at the Edinburgh Fringe.

"I cried straight away," Eftos recalls. "[Edinburgh Fringe] was the most physically, mentally exhausting thing I've done in my life.

"But it was amazing. It changed my life."

The show featured not only traditional stand-up, but Eftos flexing her acting chops too, by embodying tropes of idealised womanhood, from the bookworm to the bartender to the "femmebot".

She also drew on the way women are depicted in popular culture, including Wayne's World and Basic Instinct, with her promotional poster in the style of a Bond girl.

Now, for Aphrodite, Eftos takes on the role of the Greek goddess of love as she tries to understand why romance has proved elusive.

Dropping her armour

Aphrodite is perhaps a more vulnerable hour of stand-up than Australia's First Attractive Comedian. Eftos explains she often uses her sexuality as a kind of "armour" on stage.

"Playing the persona, it makes me feel really good," she says. "I also feel like it's armour.

"There's a part of me that doesn't want to tell [audiences] stories about bad things happening to me, because they'll think less of me."

Eftos sees her new hour as both Greek comedy and tragedy, where she's the hero who is "supposed to fall because of my hubris, my pride". (Supplied: Century)

By opening up about her experiences as a single woman and the way she is perceived by men, including being treated like a "trophy", she's dropping that armour, even just a little.

"I want to teach myself that it's not embarrassing to be vulnerable," Eftos says.

"I wish I had less shame around sex and love, or just being open and loving freely. Because there's a part of me that's like, if I let a man in, they'll take my power away."

In Aphrodite, Eftos is determined to expose that vulnerable side, drawing on something she's loved since she was young: Greek mythology.

"When I found that it was like, oh, that's my culture," she says.

It was a revelatory moment for Eftos, who, as a second-generation migrant, struggled to reconcile modern Australia with the traditional "time capsule" of Greek values she grew up with, where women were discouraged from being outspoken and expected to do the bulk of domestic labour.

"I can barely speak the language, but I learned all the shame and the guilt," Eftos says.

"There's this whole idea of trying to be a good girl and adhere to values that were passed down, and it's almost like, do these values suppress us?"

Eftos tears up talking about how scared her grandmother felt when she moved to Australia at 23, only to be engaged and married within months.

Eftos also loves Athena, the goddess of wisdom: "She's a warrior and I think that is me on stage." (Supplied: Century)

"I remember her telling me [how she met my grandfather], and I got emotional, because for me, it was like, this wasn't love, this was survival," she says.

"[Women] couldn't open bank accounts, we couldn't buy houses, we couldn't really live on our own. We had to have a man choose us in order to live, especially when you're an immigrant and you're coming to a country where you're trying to make a new life."

Eftos can't help but think how different her life is to her grandmother's at the same age.

"I have this career I'm so proud of," Eftos says. "But then it's almost like, is the reason [my career] is going so well because I don't have a stupid man ruining my life?

"Do I have to compromise to find love or to find someone that will love me? I don't want love like that."

Comedy origins

In a way, Eftos's comedy persona is a response to the ideas of womanhood she internalised growing up. She even remembers family members commenting with disdain, "Oh, you're not one of those feminists".

It was an act of protest "to feel confident about what I wear or my sexuality or what I do on stage; to be an outspoken woman".

"The persona for me was like I could say and do whatever I wanted," she says.

Who to see at the comedy festival Hannah Gadsby, Rove McManus, Aaron Chen and more of your favourite Australian comedians recommend the acts to see this comedy festival season.

She first started to adopt it when she was working as an MC at a Perth cabaret/burlesque venue.

"I'll never forget how powerful it felt to go on stage in like a little dress and lingerie and be like, you can't f***ing touch us up here," she recalls.

It was a leap from being called "Elouise the tease" in high school, when she fantasised about being like the "sexy, powerful women" of popular culture, like Britney Spears, Madonna and Janet Jackson.

She says her persona is a little bit of a response to feeling ashamed of her body then, and of desiring or wanting to be desired.

It's something she still grapples with now: "I won't tell people how I really feel in a romantic way, because I feel like that would be so humiliating."

But stand-up provided an outlet for some of these feelings, her original ditzy on-stage persona developing into the kind of woman who "annoyingly" can do anything.

Kind of like Jennifer Lopez.

"But people hate Jennifer Lopez because she can do everything," Eftos says.

"Maybe when I first started, [my character] was a bit more like [the girl that bullied you in high school].

"Now I feel like it's more me: I'm more silly and playful.

" But I find it really funny that I went from being bullied to personifying this powerful woman who says it like it is. "

Playing a character riffs on the comedy Eftos watched when she was growing up: Kath and Kim, French and Saunders, and even Monty Python and Mr Bean.

She soon turned to more traditional stand-up, from Seinfeld to Eddie Murphy, Demetri Martin, Bill Bailey, and later Natasha Leggero.

"She does high status, she wears gloves on stage, and that made me go, 'Maybe I could do this," Eftos says.

After she moves to the UK, Eftos plans to return to Australia, with the third part in what she sees as a trilogy of shows. (Supplied: Century/Jordan Kirk)

Eftos studied musical theatre and screen acting at the Western Australian Academy of Performing Arts (WAAPA), having always wanted to be a performer, acting, singing and dancing from a young age.

When she found comedy — while she was still studying, in 2017 — it just fit.

"Something about comedy felt like a magic trick and I became quite obsessed," she says.

Now, Eftos's obsession has paid off. She's made it to two Raw Comedy finals, and won awards at Sydney Comedy Festival, Adelaide Fringe, Perth Fringe World and New Zealand International Comedy Festival, not to mention the Edinburgh newcomer nod.

She plans to move to the UK, where, after her Edinburgh run last year, she opened for Aunty Donna at the Apollo and sold out a string of shows at London's Soho Theatre.

"I just think there's more over there for me, and I've just got to give it a good crack," she says.

"I'm ready for the next step."

Elouise Eftos: Aphrodite is at Sydney Comedy Festival from May 6-10 and Brisbane Comedy Festival from May 21-24.

World.title: UK police probe arson at ex-synagogue as PM decries antisemitism 'crisis'
World.content:
UK police say they are investigating a new arson incident targeting London's Jewish community, as Prime Minister Keir Starmer held talks on responding to a spate of antisemitic attacks.

Sir Keir gathered community groups, government ministers and police chiefs to his official Downing Street office for talks on a response to what he called a "crisis" following several antisemitic attacks in Britain's capital in recent weeks.

In the latest incident, firefighters were called to a former synagogue in east London early on Tuesday, where a blaze caused minor damage, the capital's Metropolitan Police said in a statement.

"Given the nature of the incident and the location being a former synagogue, the incident is being investigated by Counter Terrorism Policing London," the statement said.

British Prime Minister Keir Starmer says the UK government would introduce new legislation aimed at combating antisemitism. (Reuters: Stefan Rousseau)

There have been several incidents recently, notably in the Golders Green area of north London which is home to a large Jewish community.

Last week two Jewish men were stabbed and injured in the street. A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

In March, an arson attack in the same neighbourhood destroyed four ambulances run by the Hatzola Jewish charity.

Bottles suspected of containing petrol have been thrown at two synagogues in separate incidents.

A little-known group, the Iran-linked Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), has claimed responsibility for almost all the attacks, according to SITE Intelligence Group.

The group has also claimed attacks in other European countries.

Surging Greens party accused of antisemitism

Sir Keir told Tuesday's meeting that he would rush through new legislation to tackle "malign threats".

"Our message to Iran or to any other country that might seek to promote violence, hatred or division in society is that it will not be tolerated," he said.

"We're clear-eyed about the fact that antisemitism does not have one source alone: Islamists, far left, far right extremism, all target Jewish communities," he said.

The issue is dominating the run-up to local elections later this week, with the governing Labour Party accusing some candidates from the insurgent left-wing Greens of having made antisemitic comments.

Labour is expected to lose swathes of councillors to the Greens and other parties in Thursday's local council polls, particularly in London, as left-wing voters, many angry over the Gaza war, desert it for progressive alternatives.

Britain's Green Party, under leader Zack Polanski, is denying accusations of rampant antisemitism in its ranks. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

In recent days, Labour has stepped up attacks on the Green party, led by self-styled "eco-populist" Zack Polanski, over alleged antisemitic comments by some members.

Last month, two Green party candidates in London were arrested on suspicion of stirring up racial hatred over alleged antisemitic social media posts. They no longer appears as candidates.

Government minister Steve Reed said Tuesday the Greens had been "taken over by a lot of the hard-left people that were kicked out of Labour for antisemitism".

A Green party spokesperson on Tuesday accused Labour of being "desperate".

"Out of more than 4,500 candidates, a handful have made deeply offensive comments and they are no longer supported by the Green Party," the spokesperson added.

AFP

World.title: Trump is trying to break the OPEC oil cartel. The UAE has done exactly what he wanted
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastOPEC Opinion Trump is trying to break the OPEC oil cartel. The UAE has done exactly what he wanted Clinton Fernandes Academic and former intelligence officer May 6, 2026 — 5:02am

May 6, 2026 — 5:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The United Arab Emirates’ decision to leave the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries on May 1 exposes long-running dissatisfaction inside the group about its direction under the leadership of Saudi Arabia. It also advances Donald Trump’s goal of weakening the powerful oil bloc. The departure reflects the UAE’s own interests as well as its alignment with the United States. Along with Saudi Arabia’s potential funding cut to LIV Golf, it shows that the emerging regional order will be more transactional and less concerned with soft power. US President Donald Trump meets with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Dubai last year. Getty Images The UAE was the third-largest producer inside OPEC, which it joined in 1967. OPEC expanded in 2016 when oil prices tumbled, thanks to significant increases in US shale oil production. The group formed OPEC+ with 10 other oil-producing countries including Russia, the world’s third-largest oil producer. OPEC+ sets quotas, or production targets, for each of its members. Quotas are calculated based on members’ production capacity, oil reserves, past production levels and intense behind-the-scenes negotiations. In recent years, the UAE had invested heavily in infrastructure to increase its fossil fuel production as well as its midstream and downstream capacity. It wanted higher quotas to recoup its investments. At one point, up to a third of its pumping capability was unused, resulting in disputes that culminated in a public clash with Saudi Arabia in July 2021. It’s not the first country to be upset with Saudi Arabia’s leadership of OPEC; Indonesia left in 2016, Qatar in 2019, Ecuador in 2020 and Angola in 2023.



The UAE timed its announcement well. The supply crunch caused by the Persian Gulf crisis means its withdrawal won’t increase oil price volatility, because the closure of the Strait of Hormuz means it can’t export more oil yet, and the market was undersupplied anyway. The closure had forced regional producers including Saudi Arabia and Iraq to slash production. The UAE also approached US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to discuss currency swap lines, which would give it inexpensive access to US dollars. Currency swaps would allow the UAE central bank to support its currency or shore up its foreign reserves if foreign investors withdrew their money following Iranian attacks on its financial centre, Dubai. The US Federal Reserve used swap lines during the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic to protect the currency of its favoured central banks. Related Article Explainer

Middle East at war Its seven emirates united 50 years ago. Now the UAE faces its biggest challenge yet The UAE’s request was tentative and precautionary, not formal, but the US may be favourably disposed to help. It can let the UAE temporarily exchange its holdings of Treasury securities for US dollars through a repurchase agreement program administered by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the most influential of the 12 regional Federal Reserve banks. The US recognises that the UAE’s defection weakens OPEC, which is Donald Trump’s goal as well. It has no intention of putting the UAE in a position where it runs short of dollars and has to use Chinese yuan for oil sales and other transactions. Trump wants the dollar to remain the supreme global currency with a near-exclusive use in oil transactions. It helps, too, that an investment entity linked to the UAE’s National Security Adviser, Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed al-Nahyan, bought a 49 per cent stake in Donald Trump’s crypto venture, World Liberty Financial, for $US500 million just before the January 2026 inauguration.



The UAE has a strong commitment to countering political Islam, sharing this objective with India and Israel. It is a key partner in I2U2, the partnership with India, Israel, and the US that connects the Mediterranean Sea and the Middle East to the Indian Ocean and the Indo-Pacific region, thereby linking up with Australia’s own foreign policy stance. The UAE is pro-Israel, pro-US and hosts large US forces at al-Dhafra Air Base. It remains a key partner in the Abraham Accords, a signature Trump initiative in 2020-2021 that formalised relations between Israel and three other Arab countries, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan. When it came under Iranian missile attack, Israel sent it an Iron Dome missile defence battery with interceptors and several dozen operators. The UAE became the first country other than Israel and the US to use the system. Although the UAE acted principally in its own interests, the effect strengthens Donald Trump’s campaign to weaken the energy cartel. Venezuela, now under the government of Delcy Rodriguez, could defect as well, if the opposition party comes to power at the next election. Trump’s upending of established arrangements in Latin America and the Middle East is behind both developments. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war Middle East tensions ignite, oil surges on first day of Trump’s new ‘project’ For its part, Saudi Arabia continues to insist on OPEC+ quotas to support an oil price that helps its national budget and development goals. Although it is the largest economy in the region, its larger population and less diversified economy means that its per capita GDP is much lower than the UAE’s (US$35,000 versus US$50,000). It has signalled a wider pullback on investments that seek to increase its cultural influence, such as investing in sporting events, in favour of investments that provide monetary returns. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund bought a majority stake in English football club Newcastle United in 2021. It has also invested in boxing, wrestling, motorsports, tennis and eSports events, with an estimated involvement in 346 direct or indirect sports sponsorships and investments. It will host the soccer World Cup in 2034. Now, however, it is reassessing its support for the lucrative LIV golf competition, whose 54 holes rather than the traditional 72 were reflected in its Roman numeral-derived name. Saudi Arabia has decided to treat its sports holdings as investments that need to make a return. Soft power is less relevant in a me-first transactional world. So is anything resembling solidarity with other Gulf states.



Trump looks at the UAE with appreciation – and perhaps some wistfulness. The UAE is ruled by autocratic billionaires, not unlike his business partners. They just happen to wear long white robes rather than suits. And they don’t have to fight the midterm elections in November. Professor Clinton Fernandes is in the Future Operations Research Group at UNSW. His latest book is Turbulence: Australian Foreign Policy in the Trump Era. World.title: My SMSF is over $3 million. How should I prepare for the new super tax?
World.content:
MoneyTaxSuperannuation Opinion My SMSF is over $3 million. How should I prepare for the new super tax? Noel Whittaker Money columnist May 6, 2026 — 5:01am

May 6, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I understand the new laws that will apply an additional tax on people with superannuation balances above $3 million from the 2026/27 financial year also introduces an option for a “cost base reset” of assets. Could you explain how this works, what needs to be done and who needs to be notified? SMSF specialist Meg Heffron points out that many self-managed super funds hold assets that have risen significantly in value over time. To ensure that this past growth is not caught by the new Division 296 tax, the legislation allows trustees to reset the cost base of all CGT assets held at June 30, 2026, to their market value at that date. This is an all-or-nothing choice, so you cannot reset some assets and ignore others. Those with large super balances will need to prepare for the new Division 296 tax. Simon Letch If the trustee elects to use the reset, the fund must effectively keep two sets of records for each asset. The original cost base remains in place and is used when preparing the fund’s tax return and calculating capital gains tax in the usual way. Alongside that, a second, adjusted cost base is created based on the market value at June 30, 2026. This adjusted figure is used solely for calculating earnings under the Division 296 tax and does not affect the fund’s normal tax position.



For example, imagine a fund holding two assets at June 30, 2026. One was purchased for $4 million and is now worth $7 million, while another cost $2 million but has fallen in value to $1.5 million. If the reset is chosen, those market values become the reference points for Division 296 purposes, while the original purchase prices continue to apply for normal tax. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I want to give $65k to my teenage kids. How do I stop them spending it? Paul Benson Money contributor If the first asset is later sold for $10 million, the fund would show a capital gain of $6 million for its tax return, being the difference between the sale price and the original $4 million cost. However, for Division 296 purposes, the gain would be only $3 million, measured against the reset value of $7 million. The reverse can also occur. If the second asset is sold for $1.8 million, the fund would record a capital loss of $200,000 for tax purposes but a gain of $300,000 for Division 296 because the reset value was lower than the original cost. The detailed mechanics of how the election is to be made have not yet been released. At this stage, all we know is that it will need to be done in a format approved by the ATO, and it must be completed by the due date for lodgement of the fund’s 2026/27 tax return.



While that may be some way off (even as late as May 2028 for some funds), the relevant asset values for the adjustment will be June 30. The practical implication is that trustees need to think about whether they will opt in much earlier and will have to obtain accurate market valuations, well-supported with evidence, at that time. I’ve recently retired and have about $900,000 in super. It remains in accumulation phase and I haven’t needed to access it yet. I’m planning to add another $390,000 in non-concessional contributions in early July, using the three-year bring-forward rule. That money is currently in a term deposit. Given the current global uncertainty, would you suggest holding off on adding these funds until conditions improve, and keeping the money in a high-interest term deposit for now? Secondly, do you always recommend moving super into pension phase, even if the income is not needed? I’m concerned that converting in the current environment could have a negative impact. History tells us that time in the market is far more important than trying to time the market. If you have recently retired, you may have 25 years or more ahead of you, and over that time you will see the normal gyrations of all markets. If you have worked in the current financial year, it may be worth investigating the possibility of making a tax-deductible contribution before June 30, which could generate a useful tax refund.



Make sure your asset allocation suits your risk profile, and that you keep at least three years of planned expenses in cash or similar investments so you are never forced to sell growth assets at a bad time. As for delaying your non-concessional contribution, that becomes a judgment call, but history suggests that delaying investments in the hope of better conditions is rarely rewarded. Related Article Opinion

Hip pocket A free $1000? Not quite. Here’s how the new instant tax deduction works Dominic Powell Money Editor Your accumulation and pension accounts are usually invested in similar assets, so switching from one to the other does not materially change your market exposure. What it does change is the tax treatment. By moving to pension phase, the earnings on that portion of your super become tax-free, so in most cases there is a clear advantage in making the switch, even if you do not need the income immediately. I understand that when I make a profit on shares, I pay capital gains tax if I have held them for more than 12 months, and that there is currently a 50 per cent discount on the gain. Do I pay CGT as a separate tax on the remaining amount or is the discounted gain added to my taxable income?



A hypothetical example might help. Suppose you had $250,000 worth of shares and decided to sell $100,000 of them. If there was a capital profit of $40,000 on that parcel, the gain after the 50 per cent discount would be $20,000. That amount is added to your taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate – it is not a separate tax. The remaining shares retain their existing cost base, which is used for CGT purposes when you eventually sell them. Noel Whittaker is author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. World.title: Paying for your partner’s aged care? Don’t make this $750,000 mistake
World.content:
May 6, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lending money within families has always been fraught. Add aged care to the mix, and what starts as an act of generosity can quickly become a financial and emotional minefield. Increasingly, spouses are stepping in to fund aged care costs. It reflects a broader social shift – second and third marriages and blended families are now the norm rather than the exception. With that comes a mismatch between how the system assesses people, and how their lives are structured. Paying for your partner’s aged care costs could be a double-edged sword. Glenn Hunt Under Australia’s aged care means testing rules, couples are generally assessed on half their combined assets and income. On paper, that sounds equitable. In reality, it often isn’t. Take a common scenario. A couple meets later in life. He has modest savings and no home. She owns the house they live in and is financially comfortable, having inherited wealth from parents and a previous marriage. Her intention is clear: she wants to look after her new partner, but ultimately pass her estate to her children.



Then aged care enters the picture. Based on his half share of the assets and income, he needs to pay the market price for his aged care. In many aged care homes that means a refundable accommodation deposit (RAD) of $750,000, with the alternative being a daily accommodation payment (DAP) of $164 a day — almost $60,000 a year. Paying the RAD can ease the cash flow pressure of aged care fees, but those savings can pale into insignificance if there is a dispute. That’s just the accommodation cost. He will also need to pay the basic daily fee and based on his share of the assets and income, a hotelling fee and the non-clinical care contribution. If he pays by daily payment, his total annual costs will be more than $131,000 a year. Doing nothing is expensive, but stepping in to help isn’t straightforward either. If she chooses to pay the RAD, the numbers appear to improve. Paying the lump sum effectively offsets the DAP, saving about $60,000 a year. But there’s a trade-off: that $750,000 is no longer available to invest, and it’s not fully refunded, a retention fee of 2 per cent ($15,000) a year for five years will be deducted from it.



And then there’s the real sting in the tail: what happens when he leaves. The balance of the RAD is refundable, but it is paid to the resident’s estate – not to the person who provided the funds. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care The massive ‘care gaps’ exposing Australia’s aged care crisis Rachel Lane Money contributor Jennifer Dixon, a wills and estate specialist with Moores, says: “What began as a gesture of love and care can quickly turn into a dispute. Ideally, a loan agreement between the couple would be drawn up. Absent this, his will could direct the funds to her, but this could be challenged by other beneficiaries.” The most common issue when one spouse pays for the other’s aged care is deceptively simple: is it a gift or a loan? Paying the RAD can certainly ease the cash flow pressure of aged care fees, saving tens of thousands of dollars a year, but those savings can pale into insignificance if there is a dispute about getting a refund. It’s worth getting advice.



Rachel Lane is the author of Downsizing Made Simple, a book and website aimed at demystifying downsizing.
